To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) immunopathology is a key driver of the evolution of pathogenesis and infection-induced mortality in many infectious diseases; 2) immunopathology can be incorporated within the framework of trade-off hypothesis of disease evolution; and 3) immunopathology complicates the interpretation of the effects of public and animal health programs on the evolution of infectious diseases.

the trade-off hypothesis of the evolution of parasite virulence, which rests on the assumption of a positive correlation between pathogen exploitation and infection-induced mortality, can be extended to incorporate the detrimental effects of host immune responses, and that this extension can be used to predict the effect of immunopathology on the evolution of pathogenicity.

(1) immunopathology complicates the relationship between pathogen exploitation and host mortality, (2) immunopathology can be incorporated into the trade-off hypothesis, (3) immunopathology is likely to have different effects on the evolution of infection-induced mortality, depending on how the pathogen and host interact and (4) the trade-off hypothesis is therefore a useful framework to understand how immunopathology affects virulence evolution.
